title: Basis-set error bounds for first-quantised quantum simulation of chemistry
authors: Dominic W. Berry, Arkin Tikku, Sophia Simon, Ryan Babbush
abstract: In quantum simulation of electronic structure it is often expected that the estimate of the ground energy converges to the continuum basis limit at a rate of $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ for a basis of size $N$. This has been found in analytical and numerical studies, but without a rigorous treatment of the error in the quantities considered in quantum algorithms. Here we show the $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ scaling of the error for a wide range of cases needed for quantum simulation of chemistry. We show the error in the ground energy scales as $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ for plane-wave as well as spatial grid bases. For the spatial grid we consider both a periodic system and a non-periodic system with open boundaries. For time evolution, our bound on the error in the state itself is weaker than $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$, but we show that the error in observables scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(N^{-1})$ in important cases. In particular, we may consider a smoothed observable that describes the position of particles. We show that this error scales as $\mathcal O(N^{-5/3}+tN^{-1})$ for time $t$, again both for plane-wave and spatial grid bases. For the non-periodic grid case we use a condition that the true evolution would not result in significant leakage past the boundaries, which introduces basis error unrelated to the resolution of the discretisation. We also show the error in the kinetic energy of a particle scales as $\mathcal O((t+\log N)/N)$ for the plane-wave and grid bases. Together, these results show that $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ scaling of the error holds for many of the relevant cases for quantum algorithms (with a trivial log factor for kinetic energy).
summary: This work provides rigorous mathematical proofs for the convergence rate of quantum simulations of chemistry when using finite basis sets. It demonstrates that the error in the ground energy and several key observables scales as $O(N^{-1})$, which is a critical theoretical result for implementing quantum algorithms for electronic structure calculations.
main_problem: The paper establishes rigorous error bounds for the basis-set error when using first-quantized quantum simulation methods to calculate the electronic structure of chemical systems.
main_result: The error in the ground energy is shown to scale as $O(N^{-1})$ for both plane-wave and spatial grid bases, confirming the expected convergence rate for many relevant quantum algorithms.
method: The analysis involves comparing continuum Hamiltonian results with finite basis set representations (plane waves and spatial grids) and deriving asymptotic error bounds for various observables and time evolution.
model_or_system: The system is quantum simulation of chemistry, modeled by many-particle Coulomb Hamiltonians. The analysis covers both periodic (fixed cell) and non-periodic (isolated) boundary conditions.
key_observables: Ground energy, error in the state itself during time evolution, and errors in observables like the smoothed particle position and kinetic energy.
important_parameters: Basis size ($N$), time ($t$), momentum cutoff ($K$), and the scaling factor $\epsilon$ (related to the error tolerance).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the initial state satisfies strong regularity conditions (e.g., $|\psi_0angle \in D(H^2)$) and that the system's evolution remains well-behaved near boundaries for non-periodic cases.
figures_summary: The notes mention TABLE I summarizing principal discretization-error bounds for both periodic and non-periodic systems, detailing bounds for ground-state energy and smooth observables.
paper_structure: The paper develops the error analysis by first establishing bounds for the ground state, then extending these bounds to time evolution, and finally addressing the specific challenges posed by non-periodic boundary conditions and various observables.
why_interesting: The rigorous derivation of $O(N^{-1})$ convergence rates for key observables is crucial for designing and benchmarking quantum algorithms for chemistry, providing theoretical guarantees for resource estimation.
